classification.difficultyReason: Students must translate grid journeys into arrangements of six right and four upward moves, then recognise that paths through D split into two independently counted segments. Multiplying those segment counts and comparing with the total requires a non-trivial connection between combinatorial counting and equally likely outcomes; part (a) supplies the denominator for part (b).

spec.description: Six columns and four rows, with A at the bottom-left corner, B at the top-right corner and D two columns right and three rows up from A. The labelled-vertex feature requires TikZ rather than the blank-grid template.
spec.mathematics: A=(0,0), B=(6,4), D=(2,3); unit horizontal and vertical lattice edges.
spec.answerVisibility: All supplied grid lines, points and labels remain visible in the question edition.

children.label: a
children.prompt: In the diagram shown, in how many different ways can you get from $A$ to $B$ if you are only allowed to move to the right and upwards?

answer.short:
$210$

Choose the positions of the four upward moves among ten moves.
answer.worked:
Every complete path contains six right moves and four upward moves. Choosing the positions of the four upward moves determines the path.
$$N=\binom{10}{4}=210.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: What is the probability that a random journey from $A$ to $B$ passes through the point $D$? (Only moves to the right and up are allowed.)

answer.short:
$\frac{5}{21}$

There are 50 paths through $D$ among 210 equally likely complete paths.
answer.worked:
Take all complete paths from $A$ to $B$ as equally likely. From $A$ to $D$ requires two right moves and three upward moves; from $D$ to $B$ requires four right moves and one upward move.
$$\begin{align*}N_{AD}&=\binom{5}{2}=10\\N_{DB}&=\binom{5}{1}=5\\N_{\text{through }D}&=10\times5=50\\P(\text{through }D)&=\frac{50}{210}=\frac{5}{21}\end{align*}$$
